public.title: Sequences & Series Calculus resources | Better Grades

public.title: Order of operations with variables: what actually comes first? | Better Grades
public.description: Parentheses and exponents set the structure; multiplication, division, addition, and subtraction then move left to right within their own level.

public.title: Combining like terms without combining things that only look alike | Better Grades
public.description: Terms combine only when their variable parts match exactly. The coefficients change; the variable structure does not.

public.title: The distributive property: why the outside factor reaches every term | Better Grades
public.description: Distribution is multiplication across a sum. It expands an expression without changing its value—and it works in reverse when factoring.

public.title: Solving linear equations: keep the balance, not a bag of tricks | Better Grades
public.description: An equation stays true when the same legal operation is applied to both sides. Simplify, isolate, and check.

public.title: Variables on both sides: which side should you move them to? | Better Grades
public.description: Either side can work. Choose the direction that keeps the variable coefficient positive and the arithmetic easy to audit.

public.title: Slope is a rate of change, not just rise over run | Better Grades
public.description: Slope measures how much the output changes for each one-unit change in the input. Its sign, size, and units all carry meaning.

public.title: How to write a line equation from two points | Better Grades
public.description: Find the slope first, anchor it to either point, then convert forms only if the problem needs a different presentation.

public.title: Point-slope or slope-intercept form: which should you use? | Better Grades
public.description: Use point-slope form when a point and slope are given; use slope-intercept form when the intercept or a quick graph is the main goal.

public.title: Parallel and perpendicular slopes, with the vertical-line exception | Better Grades
public.description: Parallel nonvertical lines share a slope. Perpendicular nonvertical lines have slopes whose product is −1—but vertical and horizontal lines need separate language.

public.title: What do slope and intercept mean in a linear model? | Better Grades
public.description: The intercept is the modeled output at input zero; the slope is the predicted change in output per unit of input. Context decides whether either interpretation is sensible.

public.title: Graphing, substitution, or elimination: which system method fits? | Better Grades
public.description: Choose from the equation structure: graph when the intersection matters visually, substitute when a variable is already isolated, and eliminate when coefficients align.

public.title: Solving systems by substitution | Better Grades
public.description: Replace one variable with an equal expression, solve the resulting one-variable equation, then recover and verify the second coordinate.

public.title: Solving systems by elimination | Better Grades
public.description: Align like terms, create opposite coefficients, add the equations, and recover the variable that was deliberately removed.

public.title: One solution, no solution, or infinitely many? | Better Grades
public.description: For two linear equations, the coefficient pattern determines whether the graphs intersect once, never meet, or are actually the same line.

public.title: Compound inequalities: and, or, and the sign flip | Better Grades
public.description: Solve each condition, reverse the inequality only when multiplying or dividing by a negative, then combine by intersection or union.

public.title: Exponent rules that come from counting factors | Better Grades
public.description: The rules are compressed descriptions of repeated multiplication. Knowing where they come from prevents powers from spreading across sums illegally.

public.title: Multiplying polynomials without losing a term | Better Grades
public.description: Every term in one factor multiplies every term in the other. Organize the products, then combine like terms once.

public.title: Factor the greatest common factor before anything fancy | Better Grades
public.description: The GCF is the largest expression dividing every term. Removing it first exposes the smaller polynomial that actually needs attention.

public.title: Factoring trinomials: use product and sum, not random guessing | Better Grades
public.description: For x² + bx + c, find two numbers with product c and sum b. For ax² + bx + c, split the middle term using product ac.

public.title: Difference of squares or perfect-square trinomial? | Better Grades
public.description: Recognize the pattern from term count, signs, square roots, and the middle coefficient—then expand to confirm rather than trusting appearance alone.

public.title: Domain restrictions in rational expressions | Better Grades
public.description: A rational expression is undefined wherever its original denominator is zero. Simplifying the formula does not restore an excluded input.

public.title: Simplifying rational expressions by factors, not by terms | Better Grades
public.description: Factor completely, record excluded inputs, and cancel common factors. Individual terms separated by addition cannot be canceled.

public.title: Adding and subtracting rational expressions | Better Grades
public.description: Factor denominators, build the least common denominator, rewrite every numerator, then combine while preserving restrictions.

public.title: Solving rational equations without accepting forbidden answers | Better Grades
public.description: List restrictions, multiply every term by the least common denominator, solve the resulting equation, and reject candidates outside the original domain.

public.title: Direct or inverse variation: which model matches the relationship? | Better Grades
public.description: Direct variation keeps a constant ratio y/x; inverse variation keeps a constant product xy. The data pattern decides the model.

public.title: Simplifying radicals by pulling out perfect powers | Better Grades
public.description: Factor the radicand into a perfect power times what remains. Pull only complete groups through the radical bar.

public.title: Solving radical equations and checking for extraneous roots | Better Grades
public.description: Isolate one radical, raise both sides to the matching power, solve, and check every candidate in the original equation.

public.title: Rational exponents: the bridge between powers and roots | Better Grades
public.description: The denominator names the root and the numerator names the power. This notation lets radical expressions use the ordinary exponent rules.

public.title: Function notation: inputs, outputs, and what f(x) does not mean | Better Grades
public.description: f(x) names the output of function f at input x. The parentheses indicate evaluation, not multiplication.

public.title: Inverse function or reciprocal? The −1 notation has two different jobs | Better Grades
public.description: f⁻¹ reverses a function's input-output pairing; 1/f takes reciprocal outputs. They are generally different operations.

public.title: Evaluating algebraic expressions by substitution | Better Grades
public.description: Replace every occurrence of the variable, preserve the expression's grouping, and simplify only after the substitution is complete.

public.title: Graphing a linear equation from standard form | Better Grades
public.description: Use intercepts when they are clean, or solve for y when slope and vertical change are more informative.

public.title: Graphing linear inequalities in two variables | Better Grades
public.description: Draw the boundary, decide whether it belongs to the solution, then test a point to choose the correct half-plane.

public.title: Completing the square without guessing | Better Grades
public.description: Add the exact term that turns a quadratic expression into a perfect-square trinomial, while preserving the equation's value.

public.title: Simplifying complex rational expressions | Better Grades
public.description: Treat the stacked fraction as division, state every original restriction, and clear the small denominators with one common multiplier.

public.title: Exponential growth and decay: reading the model | Better Grades
public.description: Separate the starting amount from the repeated growth factor, then connect each parameter to a real change per time interval.

public.title: Why is the limit of sin x over x equal to 1? | Better Grades
public.description: A foundational limit whose real proof comes from geometry, not from plugging in zero and hoping.

public.title: How to evaluate an indeterminate limit | Better Grades
public.description: A decision process for 0/0 and ∞/∞ that starts with algebra before reaching for a theorem.

public.title: What continuity at a point really requires | Better Grades
public.description: Three conditions, one precise promise: nearby inputs produce nearby outputs without a break at the point.

public.title: How and when to use the Squeeze Theorem | Better Grades
public.description: Trap a difficult function between two easier functions that are forced to meet at the same limit.

public.title: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes | Better Grades
public.description: Infinity describes unbounded behavior, not a number a function eventually reaches.

public.title: What is the derivative of x to the x? | Better Grades
public.description: The base and exponent both vary, so neither the ordinary power rule nor the simple exponential rule works alone.

public.title: The Chain Rule as a structure-reading skill | Better Grades
public.description: Differentiate the outside function, keep the inside intact, then multiply by the inside rate.

public.title: Implicit differentiation without losing dy/dx | Better Grades
public.description: Differentiate an equation whose y-values are not isolated, treating y as a function of x every time it appears.

public.title: When logarithmic differentiation is the clean move | Better Grades
public.description: Use logarithms to untangle variable exponents and products or quotients with many factors.

public.title: Product Rule or Quotient Rule? | Better Grades
public.description: Choose the derivative rule from the top-level operation—and simplify first when algebra can remove the choice entirely.

public.title: Related rates: translate the geometry before differentiating | Better Grades
public.description: Connect changing quantities with one equation, differentiate with respect to time, and substitute only after the rates appear.

public.title: A calculus optimization workflow that does not skip the model | Better Grades
public.description: Turn a word problem into one objective function, then use calculus and endpoint checks to justify the best feasible value.

public.title: Linear approximation: use the tangent line as a local calculator | Better Grades
public.description: Near a known input, a smooth function behaves like its tangent line—and the derivative measures the approximation’s sensitivity.

public.title: What the Mean Value Theorem actually guarantees | Better Grades
public.description: Some instantaneous rate must match the average rate—provided continuity and differentiability hold where required.

public.title: Curve sketching from first and second derivatives | Better Grades
public.description: Build a graph from domain, intercepts, asymptotes, monotonicity, extrema, concavity, and end behavior—in that order.

public.title: u-substitution as the reverse Chain Rule | Better Grades
public.description: Replace a repeated inner expression and its derivative with one variable so the antiderivative’s structure becomes visible.

public.title: How to choose an identity for a trigonometric integral | Better Grades
public.description: The parity of sine, cosine, secant, and tangent powers tells you what to save and what to convert.

public.title: Partial fractions: decompose before integrating | Better Grades
public.description: Turn a proper rational function into simpler fractions whose antiderivatives are logarithmic or inverse-trigonometric.

public.title: Choosing the right trigonometric substitution | Better Grades
public.description: Match a quadratic radical to a Pythagorean identity so the square root simplifies instead of becoming worse.

public.title: Improper integrals are limits, not unusual notation | Better Grades
public.description: Replace infinite bounds or unbounded integrands with limits before evaluating, then decide whether the result converges.

public.title: Washer method or shell method? | Better Grades
public.description: Choose slices by geometry: perpendicular slices create washers, parallel slices create cylindrical shells.

public.title: Area between curves without guessing top and bottom | Better Grades
public.description: Find intersections, choose a slice direction, and integrate the positive geometric difference across each interval.

public.title: Where the arc-length formula comes from | Better Grades
public.description: Approximate a smooth curve by tiny line segments, then let the partition refine until the polygonal lengths converge.

public.title: Average value of a function on an interval | Better Grades
public.description: Total accumulated output divided by interval length—the continuous counterpart of an arithmetic mean.

public.title: Setting up work and fluid-force integrals | Better Grades
public.description: Slice the changing force into small contributions, express every dimension in one variable, and integrate with units attached.

public.title: Why does the harmonic series diverge? | Better Grades
public.description: Its terms approach zero, but they do so too slowly for the accumulated sum to settle.

public.title: Geometric series: convergence, sum, and structure | Better Grades
public.description: A constant ratio makes an infinite sum exactly solvable when repeated scaling shrinks toward zero.

public.title: How to choose a convergence test | Better Grades
public.description: Match the series’ structure to a test instead of cycling through tests in chapter order.

public.title: Finding a power series interval of convergence | Better Grades
public.description: Find the radius with the Ratio or Root Test, then test both endpoints separately because the general test goes silent there.

public.title: Taylor remainder: how accurate is the polynomial? | Better Grades
public.description: A Taylor polynomial is useful only with a way to control what was left out.

public.title: One-sided limits and jump discontinuities | Better Grades
public.description: A two-sided limit exists only when the function approaches the same value from the left and from the right.

public.title: Derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions | Better Grades
public.description: Recognize the inverse-trig outer function, differentiate its input, and keep the domain restrictions visible.

public.title: Newton's method: approximating roots with tangent lines | Better Grades
public.description: Use the tangent line at a current guess to generate a better root estimate, then monitor whether the iteration is actually improving.

public.title: Integration by parts: choosing u and knowing when to repeat | Better Grades
public.description: Reverse the product rule, choose the factor that simplifies under differentiation, and recognize when the method should be repeated or abandoned.

public.title: Surface area of revolution: radius times arc length | Better Grades
public.description: Build the integral from the distance to the axis and the differential arc length, then check that the chosen function stays nonnegative where required.

public.title: Ratio test or root test? Choose from the series structure | Better Grades
public.description: Use ratios for factorial and product growth, roots for whole expressions raised to n, and recognize when either test returns no decision.

public.title: Integration by parts: recognition, setup, and examples | Better Grades
public.description: Recognize integration by parts, choose u and dv, and know when another method is better.
